summary: Standing Indian Mountain's summit lookout, built by 1929, was abandoned in 1951 and removed in the 1960s; anchors for its guy wires remain.

facts.status_note: The lookout was removed in the 1960s; anchors set into rock for its guy wires remain.

access.note: The summit lies in the Southern Nantahala Wilderness of Nantahala National Forest and is reached on foot.

visit.trail_note: No tower stands. The mountain lies along the Appalachian Trail, and the easiest route to the top is a hike.

events.note: A lookout house was built on the summit.
The lookout was abandoned; the Albert Mountain tower nearby served as a replacement.
The site history says only 'In the 1960s it was removed.' The exact year is not known, so it is left null.

evidence.supports: Standing Indian Mountain is the highest point in both Macon and Clay counties.
evidence.quote: County: Macon and Clay (highpoint of both counties)

evidence.supports: The first lookout was a log cabin with a ladder giving access to its roof.
evidence.quote: The first lookout structure was a log cabin with a ladder to its roof.

evidence.supports: A lookout house was built on the summit in 1929.
evidence.quote: In 1929, a lookout house was built on the summit.

evidence.supports: The August 1936 Cherokee Scout reported that funds would pay for a new bridle trail up from Deep Gap.
evidence.quote: Funds also will make possible the construction of a new bridle trail to the summit of Standing Indian bald from the foot of the mountain at Deep Gap.

evidence.supports: The same August 1936 report said funds would pay for a new stone observation tower at the summit.
evidence.quote: A new stone observation tower will be erected at the summit of Standing Indian, which commands one of the finest views in the Nantahala mountains.

evidence.supports: The planned 1936 stone tower is recorded as unclear: it is not known what happened to the plan.
evidence.quote: In 1936, funds were being made available to construct a new trail to the top from Deep Gap and then build a new stone observation tower. Unclear what happened.

evidence.supports: The lookout was abandoned in 1951; the Albert Mountain tower served as a replacement.
evidence.quote: In 1951 the lookout was abandoned. The lookout tower on nearby Albert Mountain served as a replacement.

evidence.supports: The Albert Mountain tower replaced a wooden tower on Standing Indian Mountain.
evidence.quote: It replaced a wooden tower located nearby on Standing Indian Mountain.

evidence.supports: The lookout was removed in the 1960s, so nothing stands on the summit now.
Some evidence remains, such as anchor points set into large rocks that held the guy wires.
evidence.quote: there is some evidence around the site like anchors imbedded in large rocks for the guy wires.

evidence.supports: One account says the lookout went over a drop-off about ten feet from the summit.
evidence.quote: The lookout was said to have been pitched over the drop off ten feet from the summit.

evidence.supports: Standing Indian Mountain is inside the Southern Nantahala Wilderness.
evidence.quote: Standing Indian Mountain is located inside the Southern Nantahala Wilderness

evidence.supports: The mountain lies along the Appalachian Trail.
evidence.quote: The mountain lies along the Appalachian Trail

evidence.supports: The easiest route to the summit is a hike.
The site is listed under Macon County, U.S. Forest Service.

notes_for_editor: The WillhiteWeb site history is the main source for dates. The register describes the earlier structure as a wooden tower; the site history calls it a 1929 lookout house. The 1936 stone tower is announced, not confirmed built. The removal is given only as 'the 1960s'; the events entry now has year null because no exact year is known, so a human may want to decide whether the event should stay at all. County: WillhiteWeb lists Macon and Clay; the Forest Lookouts state list gives Macon only. The WillhiteWeb page warns that many online photos mislabel the Cowee Bald tower as this site; no photos were added.
